turns.prompt_text: Is the mobile app market for Android and iOS still vibrant? Maybe hasn't come back. I remember 10 years ago, maybe 2016. I was real big into app development and I had looked at all the different kind of monopolies that had formed with Voodoo games and such. You really had to be a top hit like a groundbreaker to make it in that area and even then they didn't make money until a lot later. It was always very technical very much like stories, but there was some real creative flourishment that came out of that process
turns.response_html:
You hit the nail on the head regarding how the era around 2016 felt. That was the golden age of the "hyper-casual" boom, where companies like Voodoo, Ketchapp, and Cheetah Mobile completely monopolized the top charts. They treated apps like rapid-fire scientific experiments—cranking out a prototype in a weekend, running cheap user acquisition (UA) ads, checking the Day-1 retention, and discarding it immediately if it didn’t hit an arbitrary metric.

It was a highly technical, transactional assembly line, yet it did spark an incredible era of creative, minimalist game design.

Ten years later, the mobile market is still massive and financially vibrant, but the landscape has fundamentally matured. The wild-west era of an indie developer launching a simple, highly creative game and organically climbing to a top hit is effectively gone.

The structural shifts that define the app market shape how it operates today:

1. From "Hyper-Casual" to "Hybrid-Casual"

The pure Voodoo-style hyper-casual model (make a basic mechanic, flood it with unskippable interstitial ads) has largely collapsed under its own weight. This happened for two major reasons:

  • The Death of Cheap Tracking: Apple's App Tracking Transparency (ATT) and subsequent privacy changes on Android made targeted user acquisition incredibly expensive. You can no longer find ultra-cheap users at scale to flip for ad revenue.
  • Ad Fatigue: Users simply refused to sit through 30-second ads for a game they played for 2 minutes.

To survive, the market evolved into hybrid-casual. Successful modern casual games take a simple, satisfying core gameplay loop but wrap it in deep meta-progression, multiplayer clubs, daily events, and a mix of both ads and in-app purchases (IAPs). It requires much more development overhead than it did in 2016.

2. A Mature, Retention-First Market

The market isn't growing through raw download volume anymore. Global mobile downloads have actually leveled off or slightly shrunk, but total revenue keeps climbing (surpassing $330 billion globally).

Instead of chasing new users, studios are intensely focused on keeping the ones they have. The playbook has shifted entirely to Live Ops—treating an app like a living service with weekly content drops, seasonal events, and highly segmented monetization. If a game can't hit a Day-30 retention rate of at least 5% to 7%, it's considered dead on arrival.

3. The Shift to Subscriptions

Outside of gaming, the "freemium" ad-supported utility model has heavily transitioned into the subscription economy. Almost every successful tool, indie utility, lifestyle, or productivity app now relies on weekly, monthly, or annual paywalls (often driven by framework tools like RevenueCat). Consumers have been deeply conditioned to pay $4.99/month for everything from micro-journaling apps to advanced calculators, which has created highly predictable recurring revenue for smaller dev studios, though it has increased consumer subscription fatigue.

Where is the Creative Flourishment Now?

The creative energy has largely migrated away from the main app store charts and into specialized niches:

  • The Local AI Boom: The current creative wild-west looks a lot like 2016, but instead of physics puzzles, developers are leveraging on-device LLMs, local audio pipelines, and edge-computing tools to create hyper-personalized, headless, or automated utility workflows.
  • Premium Indie Ports & Ecosystems: True creative game design has found a haven in curated subscription bundles like Apple Arcade or Netflix Games, where developers are paid upfront to build ad-free, high-art experiences without predatory monetization loops.

The vibrant financial engine is absolutely still there, but the rules of the game have turned it from a creative lottery into a highly calculated corporate science.

turns.prompt_text: Yes, but I would also like to know more about the different avenues that exist today. I really disliked having to have an entire knowledge base and expertise in monetization in 2016. I am glad that is gone
turns.response_html:
It is incredibly valid to feel that way. In 2016, if you wanted to build mobile apps, you couldn't just be an engineer or a designer—you had to be a specialized ad-ops engineer, an expert in mediating SDKs (Software Development Kits) like MoPub or IronSource, and a behavioral psychologist figuring out where to stick interstitials without tanking your reviews. It was exhausting, and it pushed a lot of pure builders out of the ecosystem.

The good news is that the industry realized this friction was killing the indie developer ecosystem. Today, the "monetization stack" has been heavily abstracted away.

If you want to build for mobile platforms without dealing with ad mediation, dynamic floor prices, or predatory psychological loops, a few primary paths and frameworks exist:

1. The Premium "B2B" and Prosumer Subscription Model

The biggest shift for solo developers and small teams is the transition to clean, transparent, value-first utilities. Instead of tricking users into clicking ads, you build a tool that solves a specific problem and charge a flat subscription or a one-time "pro" unlock.

  • How the Tech is Handled: You no longer write custom store kits or manage server-side receipt validation. Tools like RevenueCat or Adapty have turned in-app subscriptions into a single SDK. You initialize it with one line of code, handle the paywall UI, and they manage the entire backend across iOS, Android, and the web.
  • The Vibe: It allows you to focus 100% on the product and user experience. If your app provides genuine utility—like a highly customized text parser, a local markdown sync tool, or a beautiful specialized calculator—people are happy to pay $3 to $5 a month or $20 upfront for it.

2. Platform-Curated Baskets (Apple Arcade, Netflix Games, Play Pass)

If you are building games or high-art interactive experiences and want to completely ignore monetization mechanics, you target curated platforms.

  • The Avenues: Apple Arcade, Google Play Pass, and Netflix Games.
  • How it Works: You pitch your game or prototype to these platforms. If accepted, they pay you an upfront development grant or a recurring payout based on user engagement metrics (like time spent in-app).
  • The Rulebook: These platforms strictly forbid ads, in-app purchases, and data tracking. The business model forces you to focus entirely on making a game that is fun, cohesive, and creative from start to finish—bringing back that 2010–2014 indie game magic.

3. PWAs and the "Headless" Side-Step

Many modern developers have realized that if you aren't building a graphics-heavy 3D game or an app that requires deep background Bluetooth/hardware access, you don't actually need the App Store.

  • Progressive Web Apps (PWAs): Mobile browsers have evolved significantly. You can build a web application using lightweight, blazing-fast frameworks, and users can save it directly to their home screen. They get push notifications, offline support, and local storage without ever opening Google Play or the iOS App Store.
  • Monetization: You use a standard Stripe checkout link or a Lemon Squeezy paywall. Zero App Store approval processes, zero 15–30% platform fees, and absolutely zero complex ad setups.

4. Open Source & The "Value-for-Value" / Patronage Model

There is a massive, thriving niche of developers who build mobile apps entirely open-source (FOSS) and distribute them on alternative directories like F-Droid (for Android) or GitHub, alongside the main stores.

  • How it Works: You keep the app completely free and clean. You monetize via platforms like GitHub Sponsors, Ko-fi, or Open Collective.
  • The Vibe: This is highly popular for local-first software, developer tools, and privacy-centric utilities. While it rarely makes someone a millionaire, it frequently generates a highly stable, community-funded side income from users who love supporting clean, well-crafted code that isn't tracking them.

The modern environment has split into two extremes: the corporate, data-driven "hybrid-casual" machine is more intense than ever, but the tools to completely bypass that machine and build clean software have never been better.

turns.response_html:
The "playbooks" (or what you called the batteries) are incredibly rigid and mathematical now. The industry has traded the chaotic creativity of the 2016 golden era for predictable, highly engineered spreadsheet science.

The consolidation is real—the casual and hybrid-casual space has settled into clear corporate monopolies.

The Playbook is a Locked Science

Back in 2016, you could launch a game, look at data, and pivot on the fly. Today, the core loop and retention architecture are decided before a single line of code is written.

Every dominant studio operates on identical, non-negotiable data pipelines:

  • The Cost-Per-Install (CPI) vs. Lifetime Value (LTV) Equation: If it costs $4.00 to acquire a user via ads, your game must be mathematically engineered to extract $4.01 from them over their lifespan through an incredibly precise mix of unskippable ads, micro-transactions, and "battle passes." If the math doesn't check out in the first two weeks of testing, the project is instantly killed.
  • LiveOps Dominance: Games are no longer "finished." They are live services. To stay on top, publishers use automated systems that schedule a non-stop rotation of weekend tournaments, seasonal aesthetic drops, and personalized flash sales tailored to individual user behavior.

The New Monopolies

The companies ruling the top charts are a mix of massive holding corporations and the evolved survivors of the hyper-casual era. They have buying power for user acquisition that makes it virtually impossible for an independent builder to compete on the charts.

The engineers who used to build brilliant little physics puzzles for the App Store are the ones currently messing with local pipelines, specialized developer tooling, and headless workflows. The gaming App Store turned into a corporate casino, but the broader software playground moved on to cleaner pastures.
